title: Course Overview and Bibliography
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter answers a narrower question than the ones that follow it: not "what is a $\sigma$-algebra"
or "what does a martingale converge to", but "what is this course, and where does it sit in the
literature of measure-theoretic probability". It draws on the course's own home page and its
annotated book list, and it assumes nothing beyond ordinary undergraduate probability — the course
description below is itself the map of what the rest of the book will assume and build.

## What the course covers

STAT 205A (cross-listed as MATH 218A) is the first half of a year-long course in mathematical
probability at the measure-theoretic level, aimed at PhD students — in Statistics and Mathematics,
but also Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Business and Economics — whose thesis work will
need rigorous probability rather than the calculus-based version.

The syllabus, in the order the course states it:

- a sketch of pure measure theory (stated without responsibility for proofs — it is assumed
  background, not the subject of the course)
- the measure-theoretic formulation of probability theory itself
- the classical theory of sums of independent random variables, in particular the laws of large
  numbers
- the technical machinery that the proofs of the above need: notions of convergence, and the
  techniques for handling almost-sure convergence
- conditional distributions and conditional expectation
- discrete-time martingales
- an introduction to Brownian motion

This list is also a map onto the reference text: it "roughly coincides with Chapters 1, 2, 5 and
(first half of) 8" of Durrett's *Probability: Theory and Examples*. A reader who wants to preview
where a given topic in this book sits inside that classic reference can use this correspondence.

## The reference text

**R. Durrett**, *Probability: Theory and Examples* (4th edition), is the course's required text —
described as "the single most relevant text for the whole year's course" (this is a two-semester
sequence, 205A and 205B, and Durrett covers both). Its style is "deliberately concise", and a
number of the homework problems in the course are drawn directly from it. Concise is doing real
work in that description: Durrett is the book to read after a topic has already been introduced
some other way, not the book to meet a topic in for the first time.

## Filling in the measure theory

Because the course only sketches measure theory rather than building it, two books are recommended
specifically to fill that background in, for a reader who has not already seen it:

- **P. Billingsley**, *Probability and Measure* (3rd edition) — "a more careful and detailed
  treatment of some of the topics of this semester, in particular the measure-theory background."
- **R. Leadbetter, S. Cambanis, V. Pipiras**, *A Basic Course in Measure and Probability: Theory
  for Applications* — a newer book with the same purpose, "a careful treatment of the measure-
  theory background."

## Other books at the same level

The course page also gives a personal, annotated tour of other books that cover roughly the same
"first-year graduate" ground as Durrett. Kept here because the assessments are the instructor's own
and are useful in deciding which book to reach for and why, not because any of their content is
reproduced in this course:

- **D. Khoshnevisan**, *Probability* — "a well-written concise account of the key topics."
- **R. Bhattacharya and E. C. Waymire**, *A Basic Course in Probability Theory* — "another
  well-written account, mostly on the 205A topics."
- **K. L. Chung**, *A Course in Probability Theory* — covers much of the same ground, "more
  leisurely than Durrett and more focused than Billingsley."
- **D. Williams**, *Probability with Martingales* — "a uniquely enthusiastic style," concise, and
  built around the usefulness of martingales specifically.
- **Y. S. Chow and H. Teicher**, *Probability Theory: Independence, Interchangeability,
  Martingales* — "uninspired exposition," but useful for variations on technical inequalities for
  sums and for martingales.
- **R. M. Dudley**, *Real Analysis and Probability* — "the best account of the functional analysis
  and metric space background relevant for research in theoretical probability."
- **B. Fristedt and L. Gray**, *A Modern Approach to Probability Theory* — 700 pages, covering a
  broad range of probability and stochastic processes beyond this course.
- **L. Breiman**, *Probability* — "classical; concise and broad coverage."
- **O. Kallenberg**, *Foundations of Modern Probability* — a compendium in the style of Loève's
  classical text; a reference or second-pass book rather than a first introduction, since it is
  light on examples.
- **J. B. Walsh**, *Knowing the Odds: An Introduction to Probability* — a concise treatment with
  "quite challenging exercises developing part of theory."
- **G. Roussas**, *An Introduction to Measure-Theoretic Probability* — a recent treatment of the
  classical content.
- **S. Venkatesh**, *The Theory of Probability: Explorations and Applications* — intertwines
  undergraduate and graduate topics for an applied audience.
- **I. Florescu**, *Probability and Stochastic Processes* — 550 pages, broad coverage including an
  introduction to stochastic differential equations.

## Lecture notes referred to but not included here

The course page points to three further sets of lecture notes, none of which are part of the
material converted for this chapter:

- lecture notes by **Sinho Chewi**, hosted alongside the course's own pages;
- lecture notes by **Jim Pitman**, keyed to the Durrett text and covering more ground than this
  course does;
- lecture notes by **Amir Dembo**, for the equivalent Stanford sequence (Stat 310AB).

A reader who wants a second exposition of any topic below, in a different author's voice, should
look there rather than expect it reproduced in this book.

- Book list and all quoted assessments of individual texts: `03-books.md`, the "Books" section of
  the same course page.
- Referred to but not supplied: the weekly schedule, the eleven homework assignments, and the three
  sets of external lecture notes (Chewi, Pitman, Dembo) named above.
- Administrative logistics on the course page (class time and room, office hours, grading split,
  email conventions) are omitted as course administration rather than course content.
